attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, stated as his own aside.

semantics.note: An unhedged present-state observation with two parts: tokenmaxxing has ended, and companies have started limiting token budgets. The normalisation matches both.

contract.note: The plain reading (a broad shift from rewarding token use toward spending controls, not every company stopping) is an ordinary, fair reading of 'come to end'. The two-month window comes from the post's own framing.

evidence.note: Fortune, May 28: many companies pulling back, Meta removed its leaderboard, Microsoft cancelled subscriptions, Uber blew its budget. It concludes the days of tokenmaxxing are over.
Bloomberg, June 2: Walmart capped use of an AI agent and Uber set $1,500 monthly per-tool limits, both before June 9. Direct evidence of company restrictions.
The Week, May 29: some backers, such as a Sequoia partner, still promote tokenmaxxing. This is advocacy, not representative evidence that it remained the prevailing practice.

reviews.rationale: Reporting from before June 9 by Fortune and Bloomberg documents restrictions and pullbacks at several large firms (Meta, Microsoft, Uber, Walmart), and Fortune itself says the days of tokenmaxxing are over. On the contract's plain reading, that meets the support condition. Continued advocacy (e3) does not show the practice still prevailed. No representative survey exists, so the 'ended' part rests on reporting rather than measurement.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: A compound observation: Mythos is released, and at the same time tokenmaxxing has ended and budgets are being limited. 'Just as' is about timing, and the revision rightly drops any causal claim.

contract.note: Reading 'Mythos' as the safeguarded Mythos-class model follows from his next sentence about adding guardrails. The tokenmaxxing reading is the ordinary one: a broad trend, not universal.

evidence.note: Anthropic, May 22: it had not yet released Mythos-class models to the public because safeguards were inadequate. This sets the earlier position but does not show the outcome.
Anthropic's June 9 launch: Fable 5, the same model as Mythos 5 with safeguards, is available everywhere, while Mythos 5 stays restricted. Primary release record for the release part.
Bloomberg via Willison, June 3: Uber caps per-tool token spending. Shows one company restricting; it does not show a broad end to tokenmaxxing.

reviews.rationale: The release part holds: by June 9 a safeguarded Mythos-class model (Fable 5) was generally available after the earlier withholding. For the spending part, this packet shows only Uber's limits, so the broader trend and 'tokenmaxxing has ended' are not established here. Nothing contradicts them; the evidence is simply thin. The result is mixed: the release holds and the token-budget trend is unresolved on this evidence.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: The factual core is that guardrails were added and the model released. 'Tacked on' is a dismissive characterisation and is rightly not scored.

contract.note: Counting a safeguarded Mythos-class model under a different product name is fair given his wording about guardrails and 'anyone can now use it'.

evidence.note: AWS release post, June 9: Fable 5 brings Mythos-level capabilities, with safeguards that route risky prompts to another model, and is generally available. Distribution-partner release documentation, as the contract allows.

reviews.rationale: AWS's release record from June 9 shows that a Mythos-class model with added safeguards became generally available, while the unrestricted Mythos 5 stayed limited to vetted users. That meets the support condition. How effective the safeguards are, or how much work they took, is not tested.
